newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Coffee's new highs dominate commodity markets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Coffee's new highs dominate commodity markets.

text.p: London coffee futures hit their highest for a year on Tuesday, extending a rally in the world market that has already worked through to price rises in the shops.
Elsewhere in commodity markets, copper led gains on the London Metal Exchange but, like coffee, eased on profit-taking late in the European day.

The London benchmark July robusta coffee futures contract jumped to $1,835 a tonne shortly after the open on the back of a sharp New York rally by arabica type beans on Monday. It ended at $1,815 but analysts said the market could rise again.
Robustas, used mainly in soluble or instant brews, have risen by more than 50 percent since the start of the year on worries about tight supply. New York arabica futures have doubled.
"Traders have no stocks to speak of and silos are empty," said Thomas Gehring, raw materials buyer at leading German roaster (processor) Kraft Jacobs Suchard.
The rally reignited on Monday when brokerage Merrill Lynch said prices could reach record highs ahead of new crop shipments this autumn.
"New York is still firmly on the uptrend," added a London trader who said that any retracement would be shortlived amid jitters ahead of the upcoming Brazil frost season.
Traders have not forgotten the two severe frosts in 1994, one in June and another in July, which damaged the Brazilian crop and, followed by a drought, caused prices to quadruple.
London Metal Exchange copper had a brief shot at a two month high of $2,433 per tonne early in the day's trading but profit-taking pulled it down to settle some $7 ahead at $2,413.
Funds bought copper against a backdrop of data suggesting that demand is brisk.

The other base metals hovered around opening levels with the exception of tin which was sharply lower. Tin fell some $140 to $5,730 per tonne by the afternoon, although traders said there was little fundamental news provoking the sell-off.

In other markets on Tuesday, benchmark North Sea Brent Blend crude oil took a breather after a rise of almost $2 per barrel over the last five days in what traders characterised as a day of consolidation.
The price of gold eased to hover about $2 below key resistance of $350 an ounce.
The big fundamental news in the precious metals sector was an announcement from Moscow that a five-month delay to Russian platinum and palladium exports could soon be over.
The rare white metals lost ground initially when Russian officials confirmed export talks with Japan had begun but recovered later.
"It's a very jittery market although the only logical direction is downwards," one dealer said.
Platinum was valued at $388.75/$389.75 down $7.50 and palladium was $4.00 off at $169.509/$170.50.
Wheat futures on the Chicago Board of Trade were several cents lower at midsession around $3.95 per bushel on bearish U.S. Department of Agriculture weekly crop condition ratings.
USDA said that as of Sunday, the U.S. winter wheat crop was 53 percent good to excellent, above 50 percent in that category the previous week.
Also, the market was still reeling from a collapse on Monday Monday which was tied to USDA's May crop production and supply/demand reports.
London cocoa futures closed lower with July perched on psychological support at 1,000 stg per tonne after slipping to a one-week low earlier in the session.
